ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The left side of the circuit is marked with a 3V voltage, with the upper-left terminal positive and the lower-left terminal negative; on the upper-left wire there is a 2A current arrow pointing to the right, entering the upper middle node. This upper middle node connects downward to resistor R1, reaching the lower common node; at the same time, this node goes right through resistor R2 and connects to the upper-right node. On the right side there is a vertical resistor R3, with the upper end of R3 marked positive and the lower end marked negative, the voltage is 1V, and its lower end is connected to the bottom common node. Reasoning: R1 is connected between the 3V upper node and the bottom common node, so the voltage across R1 is 3V. R2 is connected between the 3V upper node and the 1V node at the upper end of R3, so the voltage across R2 is 3V - 1V = 2V. It is known that the power of R2 is 2W, so the current through R2 is I_R2 = P/V = 2/2 = 1A. At the upper node, 2A current enters and divides into the R2 branch and the R1 branch, so I_R1 = 2A - 1A = 1A. Thus R1 = V_R1 / I_R1 = 3V / 1A = 3Ω.

Thus I_R1 = 2 A - 1 A = 1 A. Since R1 has 3 V across it, R1 = 3/1 = 3 ohms.

method.method_draft: First describe the image as a two-branch network across the 3 V left terminals: one branch is R1, and the other branch is the series path R2-R3. The total equivalent resistance seen at the left port is R_eq = 3 V / 2 A = 1.5 ohms. The voltage across R2 is read from the node labels as 3 V - 1 V = 2 V. With P_R2 = 2 W, R2's branch current is I = P/V = 1 A. Since that same current flows through the series R2-R3 branch and the whole branch has 3 V across it, the right-hand branch equivalent resistance is 3 V / 1 A = 3 ohms. Now solve the parallel relation 1/1.5 = 1/R1 + 1/3, giving R1 = 3 ohms.
